section_summary: This section covers intelligence reports, diplomatic despatches, and State Department memoranda from late August 1941 through early 1942, centering on the collapse of Prince Konoe's third cabinet and the accession of General Hideki Tōjō. The documents assess Tōjō's military background and cabinet personnel while debating whether Japan would strike northward against Soviet Siberia or advance southward toward Thailand and the Netherlands East Indies. Also included are detailed evaluations of Japan's acute raw material shortages and economic strain, FBI and G-2 field intelligence on Manchurian infrastructure and Japanese domestic morale, and a Swiss consular dispatch reviewing Dr. Lily Abegg's sociological study 'Yamato' for Allied propaganda use.

subfiles.about: A confidential survey analyzing Japan's foreign relations with Southeast Asia, the Soviet Union, Thailand, and the United States, as well as domestic economic strains.
subfiles.summary: The report reviews Japan's expansionist southward advance toward the Netherlands East Indies and the failure of commercial negotiations in Batavia following Dutch resistance and Allied export restrictions. It examines Soviet-Japanese border disputes along the Khalkha River, fisheries agreements, Sakhalin concessions, and the strategic vulnerability of Vladivostok and northern supply routes. The survey also analyzes Japanese encroachment into Thailand, growing tension with the United States over assets freezes and the oil embargo, and severe domestic economic problems including inflation, tax burdens, and commodity shortages. It concludes that Japan stands between competing expansionist policies toward tropical resources in the south or maritime Siberia in the north, facing eventual economic collapse and military disaster if confronted by the ABCD powers.
subfiles.title: Japan: Political - Foreign Relations and Domestic Survey

subfiles.about: A military intelligence memorandum reporting the resignation of the Konoe Cabinet and analyzing its likely causes and Axis orientation.
subfiles.from: Sherman Miles, Brigadier General, U.S. Army, Acting Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2
subfiles.summary: General Miles reports Konoye's cabinet fell over Toyoda's failure to ease US sanctions; he expects a pro-Axis, Army-dominated turn and Army exploitation of any Soviet weakness. State's slip notes the estimate differs from Far Eastern Division's.
subfiles.title: Resignation of the Konoye Cabinet

subfiles.about: A military intelligence profile assessing the background, temperament, and foreign policy orientation of newly designated Premier Hideki Tōjō.
subfiles.from: Sherman Miles, Brigadier General, U.S. Army, Acting Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2
subfiles.summary: General Miles reports Tojo designated Premier; he is anti-foreign, determined, hostile to Russia and an admirer of German methods, and will likely form an aggressively nationalistic, pro-Axis cabinet.
subfiles.title: Japan's New Premier

subfiles.about: A State Department assessment analyzing the political causes behind the fall of the Konoe Cabinet and predicting Japan's immediate military moves.
subfiles.from: William R. Langdon, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Langdon says Konoye fell because the military rejected conditions for adjusting relations with the US, including concessions on China. It does not foreshadow a Siberian attack; a new venture would more likely target Thailand.
subfiles.title: Fall of Konoye Cabinet

subfiles.about: A State Department biographical roster detailing the ministerial appointments in the newly formed cabinet of Premier Hideki Tōjō.
subfiles.from: William R. Langdon, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Langdon evaluates Tojo's cabinet, with Tojo holding War and Home. Foreign Minister Togo has Berlin and Moscow experience and a conciliatory Russia approach; Kishi brings state capitalism from Manchukuo.
subfiles.title: Cabinet of Premier Eiki Tojo

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet indexing a strictly confidential telegram from Ambassador Grew regarding Prince Konoe's resignation and the appointment of a new cabinet.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Telegram No. 1640 (October 17, 1941; 711.94/2375): Konoye's resignation and the successor cabinet.
subfiles.title: Resignation of Prince Konoye and Appointment of a New Cabinet

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet indexing a telegram from Ambassador Leahy in Vichy reporting French diplomatic views on General Tōjō's policies.
subfiles.from: William D. Leahy, U.S. Ambassador to France (Vichy)
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Vichy Telegram No. 1307 (October 17, 1941): Count Ostroróg on probable policies of the new Tojo cabinet (740.0011 European War 1939/16909).
subfiles.title: Probable Policies to be Pursued by the New Japanese Cabinet, Headed by General Tojo

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet indexing a telegram from Ambassador Grew analyzing American public perspectives on the Japanese cabinet transition.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Grew's Telegram No. 1661 (October 20, 1941): the American public may not have the cabinet change in accurate perspective (711.94/2382).
subfiles.title: Significance of Japanese Cabinet Change

subfiles.about: A telegram from Tokyo reporting the installation of former Finance Minister Seihin Ikeda as a member of the Privy Council.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Grew relays a Japan Advertiser report that Seihin Ikeda was installed as a Privy Council member.
subfiles.title: Installation of Seihin Ikeda as Member of the Privy Council

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet indexing a document submitted by Bishop James E. Walsh regarding the Japanese Government's position in relations with the United States.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a confidential memorandum Bishop Walsh left with Hull on November 15, 1941, on the Japanese Government's position on US relations (711.94/2540-10/35).
subfiles.title: Position of Japanese Government with Regard to Present Relations with the United States

subfiles.about: A State Department biographical memorandum evaluating General Hideki (Eiki) Tōjō's career, temperament, and foreign policy orientation for the Secretary of State.
subfiles.from: William R. Langdon, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Langdon profiles Tojo, taciturn and conservative, who supported Konoe's talks with the US; his premiership may continue Konoe's policies. Hamilton calls him an able soldier of strong convictions.
subfiles.title: General Eiki Tojo

subfiles.about: A Department of State charge slip recording the withdrawal of the enclosure to document 894.00/1142.
subfiles.summary: Charge slip: enclosure to file 894.00/1142 charged out to Hendrick van Oss on October 22, 1945.
subfiles.title: Charge Slip for File 894.00/1142
subfiles.to: Hendrick van Oss, Division of Eastern European Affairs

subfiles.about: An intelligence memorandum transmitting a secret report on internal Japanese politics, German fifth-column activities, and Emperor Hirohito's intervention.
subfiles.from: Robert T. Pell, Division of Current Information (forwarding submission by Captain James Roosevelt)
subfiles.summary: Pell forwards John Thompson's claims that Hirohito took direct Army control to suppress pro-Nazi revolts, with Suetsugu removed and Nakano jailed. German advisers urge a Siberian attack; Pacific peace needs prolonged diplomacy.
subfiles.title: Intelligence Statement on German Influence and Political Conditions in Japan
subfiles.to: George A. Atcheson, Jr., Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum analyzing Japan's strategic dilemma after the fall of the Konoe Cabinet and predicting an early assault on Siberia.
subfiles.from: Frederick A. Schuler, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Schuler argues the Konoye cabinet's fall shows Japan abandoned accommodation with the US, pressed by asset freezes and German urging, and will likely thrust into Soviet Siberia before winter.
subfiles.title: Significance of the Fall of the Konoye Cabinet

subfiles.about: A memorandum circulating confidential Dutch East Indies intelligence on the domestic plot behind the Konoe resignation and urging continued economic sanctions.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Adviser on Political Relations (forwarding memorandum from Baron van Boetzelaer)
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck circulates a Netherlands East Indies memorandum: the Konoye resignation was triggered by a Black Dragon plot against Hiranuma, bringing in Tojo; undiminished embargoes are the only guarantee against war.
subfiles.title: Dutch East Indies Views on the Tojo Cabinet and Economic Sanctions
subfiles.to: Cordell Hull, Secretary of State / Sumner Welles, Under Secretary of State

subfiles.about: A memorandum recording an interview with Otis Elevator Company representatives on acute industrial shortages, transport paralysis, and living conditions in Japan.
subfiles.from: William R. Langdon, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Langdon summarizes detailed testimony from Mr. Grandgerard, Tokyo representative of the Otis Elevator Company, who left Japan in late September 1941. Grandgerard describes severe shortages of steel, copper, rubber, tin, and lubricating oils, stating that army factory expansions and tunnel projects stalled because essential wiring, motors, and reinforcing bars were unobtainable. He notes that strict rationing and family burdens have caused widespread undernourishment and declining physical stamina among adult males of military age. Grandgerard concludes that Japan's exhausted industrial base and weakened population cannot sustain modern warfare, but warns that continuing economic isolation could provoke a desperate, short-lived outward explosion within a year.
subfiles.title: Conditions in Japan: Interview with Representatives of the Otis Elevator Company

subfiles.about: An FBI transmission enclosing an eyewitness report by a returned missionary on Japanese police surveillance and military targets in Manchuria.
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.summary: Hoover transmits to Assistant Secretary Berle a confidential five-page report prepared by a recently returned Canadian missionary regarding living conditions in Manchuria. The report describes intrusive surveillance by Japanese Special and Military Police in Siping (Ssupingkai), severe rationing of coal and flour, and deep-seated anti-Japanese resentment among Chinese and Korean inhabitants. It also provides strategic military intelligence, detailing vulnerable railway bridges, coal mines at Fushun and Hsian, steel plants at Anshan and Benxi, army barracks, and naval installations at Port Arthur, Rajin, and Chongjin.
subfiles.title: Living Conditions and Military Vulnerabilities in Manchuria
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle, Jr., Assistant Secretary of State

subfiles.about: A War Department G-2 intelligence report summarizing observations on Japanese industrial mobilization, public morale, and strategy by businessman John M. Reifsnider.
subfiles.from: Military Intelligence Division, War Department General Staff
subfiles.summary: G-2 report on John Reifsnider, a Tokyo resident from 1904 to 1941: pro-Japanese, doubts US-Japan war, predicts an attack on Soviet Manchuria, reports high morale and vulnerable power plants. Routing slips note conflicting assessments.
subfiles.title: Military Intelligence G-2 Report on Japanese Conditions and Morale

subfiles.about: An FBI memorandum compiling intelligence on Japanese naval dissension, troop and arms movements, resource targets in Borneo, and chemical weapons production.
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.summary: Hoover submits a confidential intelligence compilation detailing diverse Japanese political, military, and economic developments. The report covers Yokohama Specie Bank director Imagawa's comments on plans to seize Borneo if oil supplies remain blocked, the evacuation of Japanese families from Java, and naval refusal to intercept American tankers sailing to Vladivostok. It also reports Admiral Sankichi Takahashi's public doubts about a German victory, reports by Nanking envoy Wu Yi-ping on right-wing pressure against the cabinet, Japanese flour milling quotas, iron sand refining for vanadium and cobalt, and the manufacture of arsenic poison gases at the Sumitomo Chemical works in Niihama.
subfiles.title: Miscellaneous Intelligence Concerning Japanese Political, Military, and Industrial Matters
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle, Jr., Assistant Secretary of State

subfiles.about: A consular despatch transmitting and reviewing Dr. Lily Abegg's book 'Yamato' on Japanese national character, health deficiencies, and psychological vulnerabilities for propaganda use.
subfiles.from: James B. Stewart, American Consul General, Zürich
subfiles.summary: Consul General Stewart transmits a copy and translation of a Swiss review of Dr. Lily Abegg's 1936 book 'Yamato: Der Sendungsglaube des Japanischen Volkes' for possible use by American public information and propaganda bodies. Stewart notes that Abegg, a Swiss-German journalist suspected of working for German intelligence, possessed deep knowledge of Japan and that copies of the book were rapidly bought up by Germans in Switzerland upon the outbreak of hostilities. The enclosed review from Die Weltwoche examines Abegg's critique of Japanese national weaknesses, including pervasive ill-health, widespread tuberculosis, peasant poverty under exploitative land tenure, poor nutrition, high suicide rates, and fanatical devotion to the concept of 'Yamato Damashii'.
subfiles.title: Book on Japan for Possible Use by the Committee on Public Information: 'Yamato' by Dr. Lily Abegg
